sentences.text: The next morning, after the morning chanting and after breakfast, Grandfather Rinpoche brought Tenzin into his small cell.
It was very simple — a wooden bed, a low table, a butter lamp, a small shelf of books.
Grandfather Rinpoche sat cross-legged on a cushion on the floor.
Tenzin sat across from him.
Between them, on the low table, Grandfather Rinpoche placed a small object wrapped in soft red silk.
"This," he said, "has been in our family for four hundred years.
It was carved by the grandmother of my great-great-great-grandfather.
That was in 1626.
She carved it from a piece of hard black wood — a wood called sengchen, that grows only in one small valley high in the mountains.
She was a woodcarver.
She carved many things in her life.
This was one of her small ones.
But it is the only one of hers that has stayed with our family.
Everything else has been lost, or given away, or has broken.
Only this remains."
He unwrapped the silk.
Inside was a small carved snow lion.
It was maybe as big as Tenzin's palm.
It was carved from dark, almost black wood, and it had been rubbed smooth over four hundred years — you could see the marks of many hands.
It had a serious face.
It had a small mane.
It had four small feet planted firmly.
It looked, Tenzin thought, exactly like what a snow lion should look like — an ancient mountain creature, half real and half not, standing on its rock in the wind.
"The snow lion," said Grandfather Rinpoche, "is one of our four dignities.
Do you know the four dignities?" Tenzin said, "The tiger, the snow lion, the garuda, and the dragon." "Yes," said Grandfather Rinpoche.
"Very good.
And the snow lion — the snow lion represents joyful energy.
Not simple happiness — the joy that comes from being fully alive.
The joy of a wild thing running in the snow.
My grandmother's grandmother carved this snow lion, my father told me, in the winter that her own son died.
He was small.
He died of a fever.
And she carved this — she carved joyful energy, out of the hardest wood she could find — because she needed to remember that joy still existed in the world, even when her son had died in it.
That is why she made it.
Small joyful mountain creature, made in the middle of the biggest grief of her life."
Grandfather Rinpoche paused.
He said, "Since then, it has passed from parent to child.
Not always to the oldest.
To the one — the one who seemed to need it.
My grandmother's grandmother gave it to her surviving daughter.
That daughter gave it to her younger son.
And so on.
Twelve generations.
Every time — a child who seemed to need to know that joyful energy was a real thing.
That the world is a joyful place, at bottom, even when it is also sad.
That is the rule."
"I got it," said Grandfather Rinpoche, "from my mother, when I was ten.
She gave it to me because she said I was a very serious child, and she wanted me to remember that seriousness was not the whole thing.
She said — you can be a serious person and also a joyful person.
Both at once.
This snow lion is here to remind you of both.
I have had it for sixty-six years now.
And now I am giving it to you."
Tenzin lifted the small snow lion carefully.
It was heavier than it looked.
The wood was so dark it was almost like stone.
He turned it over in his palms.

On the bottom, in very small carved letters, was the initial that the great-great-great-grandmother had carved when she made it — a single character in an old Bhutanese script that Tenzin could not fully read.
He held it in his palm.
He said, "But Grandfather — why me.
Am I — am I a serious child." Grandfather Rinpoche smiled.
He said, "Yes, Tenzin.
You are a very serious child.
Do you not know that." Tenzin thought.
He said, "Maybe.
Yes."
"You have been a serious child since you were small," said Grandfather Rinpoche.
"Everyone in the family has noticed.
Your mother has noticed.
She and I have talked about it.
She said to me, years ago — Tenzin is like you.
He thinks too much.
He does not have enough joy.
I have watched you every summer to see if she was right.
She was right.
You do have a serious mind.
It is a good mind.
It will serve you well.
But — you need this.
You need the snow lion.
To remind you that joy is a real thing too, and that you are allowed to have it.
That is why I am giving it to you."
Tenzin said, "Grandfather.
May I ask something." Grandfather Rinpoche said, "Anything." Tenzin said, "When you gave up — when you became a monk.
After Grandmother died.
Was that — was that serious, or was that joyful.
Or was it both." Grandfather Rinpoche was silent for a long moment.
Then he said, "That is exactly the question.
And nobody has ever asked me that in forty-one years.
I am glad it is you who is asking me.
It was both, Tenzin.
When I came here, I was in a lot of grief.
My wife had died.
My daughter was going to be raised by her aunt.
I did not know what to do with myself.
I came here because I needed the silence.
That was the serious part.
That was the grief part."
"But then — over the years — I found that the silence had joy in it too.
That the mountains had joy in them.
That praying with the other monks in the early morning had joy in it.
That the small work of tending the garden had joy in it.
I did not expect this.
I had come here to be sad.
Slowly, without meaning to, I became — happy.
Not in a happy-ending way.
In a — quiet way.
In the way the snow lion is happy on the mountain in the snow.
Fully alive.
That was what happened.
That is why I am still here.
I have been very happy in this monastery.
Even when I have missed you all, in the valley — I have been happy."
